mcqs.question: A candidate says "the OS manages the computer." What's missing from a complete answer?
options: That it does this via two distinct jobs: acting as resource manager and as abstraction layer
That it only runs on servers, not personal computers
That it is written entirely in assembly language
That it requires a graphical interface to function
mcqs.explanation: "Manages the computer" is vague; naming both the resource-manager role (arbitrating shared hardware) and the abstraction-layer role (hiding hardware detail) is what a precise answer includes. OSes run everywhere, are mostly written in C with some assembly, and many (servers, embedded) have no GUI at all.

mcqs.question: What does "multiprogramming" originally refer to, as distinct from "multitasking"?
options: Keeping several jobs in memory so the CPU always has work available, without any expectation of fast switching
Writing a program in multiple programming languages
Running the same program on multiple CPU cores simultaneously
Fast enough switching between jobs that it appears concurrent to users
mcqs.explanation: Multiprogramming's original goal was simply avoiding an idle CPU while one job waits on I/O — it says nothing about switching speed. Fast, concurrent-feeling switching is multitasking. Neither term is about language choice or multi-core parallelism specifically.

mcqs.question: In the hardware/kernel/system-programs/applications stack, which layer has direct, privileged access to hardware?
options: System programs, because they ship with the OS
Applications, because they issue read and write calls
The kernel, and only the kernel
All layers have equal hardware access by default
mcqs.explanation: Only the kernel runs with the privilege to touch hardware directly; system programs and applications alike must go through it via system calls. Shipping alongside the OS doesn't grant a system program special hardware access.

mcqs.question: Why is it inaccurate to say "Linux is the operating system" without qualification?
options: Because Linux cannot run without a graphical desktop environment installed
Because Linux only refers to the kernel; the OS most people run is that kernel plus a large GNU/userland stack
Because Linux is not open source
Because the term "Linux" refers exclusively to a specific hardware architecture
mcqs.explanation: Linux, strictly, is a kernel; a runnable OS is that kernel bundled with a shell, libraries, compilers, and utilities largely from GNU — hence "GNU/Linux." Linux runs headless on most servers, is open source, and isn't tied to one architecture.

mcqs.question: What's the precise distinction between a VM and a container, in OS terms?
options: A container is just a smaller, compressed virtual machine image
A VM virtualizes hardware beneath a full guest OS; a container isolates namespaces and cgroups within one shared host kernel
There is no meaningful technical difference between the two
Containers require a hypervisor while VMs never do
mcqs.explanation: A VM's hypervisor presents virtual hardware to a complete guest OS with its own kernel; a container shares the host kernel and is isolated purely through kernel features (namespaces, cgroups) — no guest kernel or virtual hardware involved. It's the reverse of requiring a hypervisor: VMs need one, containers don't.

mcqs.question: A "noisy neighbor" problem on a shared cloud host — one tenant's workload degrading another's latency — is best understood as a failure of what?
options: The network card's firmware
The abstraction-layer job, specifically the file abstraction
The application's own code, unrelated to the underlying platform
The resource-manager job, at the hypervisor layer instead of within a single OS
mcqs.explanation: Noisy-neighbor issues are the same resource-arbitration failure an OS scheduler prevents on one machine, just occurring one layer up at the hypervisor between VM tenants. It isn't a firmware, file-abstraction, or purely application-level issue.
